thought.text: I've identified the dev compose bugs. The guide's primary Quick Start uses the production compose, which has correct nginx mounts and `printf`-based QGIS config. Let me first fix the shared `init.sh` bug (it references tables that don't exist until Django migrations run, always failing on fresh init).

reasoning_content:
There's a leftover "angry_antonelli" container from one of my timed out docker run tests. Let me clean it up.

Now let me examine the production compose for the same init.sh bug. The prod db uses the same init.sh which fails on model_permission/route_permission. But wait - in the dev stack, db started healthy after the first failure because the data dir was already initialized. Actually the init.sh failure caused the whole db container to exit during the first run. On retry, since postgres data dir already existed, initdb was skipped and init.sh wasn't re-run, so db became healthy.

Actually wait, let me re-read. The init container uses `./postgres/data` bind mount. On first `up`, initdb ran, then init.sh ran and failed at the REVOKE, causing exit 3. On second `up`, the data dir existed so initdb skipped, and init.sh also skipped (docker-entrypoint only runs initdb.d scripts when initializing a new cluster). So db became healthy. So the init.sh bug is "self-healing" after first attempt, but during the first `up -d`, dependencies fail.

Actually the important insight: init.sh's REVOKE failure is a genuine repo bug, but it only affects the FIRST init. The extension creation (postgis, pgrouting, dblink, pgcrypto) succeeded BEFORE the failure. And the QGIS user grants succeeded. So the DB is actually fine after retry — the pgrouting extension got created, so the dockerfile change provided pgrouting.

Hmm wait — in my bookworm Dockerfile I removed the postgis base image and installed postgis + pgrouting packages. init.sh created extensions successfully. Good.

But actually, should I fix init.sh? The REVOKE failure is triggered because the QGIS user variables are set. If QGIS_DB_USER/PASSWORD were empty, init.sh wouldn't run that block. The dev README example sets QGIS_DB_USER. Let me consider: this is a pre-existing bug that causes first-run failure. For a clean installation, the db exits on first `up`. This would make `docker-compose up -d` report failure. But a second `up -d` works. That's fragile.

Let me reconsider. The task: install software. The guide's quick start: `cd deployment && docker-compose up -d --build`. Let me focus on getting the production stack working, which is what the guide describes.

But production compose also has the same init.sh bug, plus tileserver needs germany.mbtiles (not in repo), plus wireguard needs privileged capabilities, plus qgis projects. Let me think about which stack is more achievable.

Actually, let me not over-engineer. The guide offers 3 methods. Let me try the production method (the primary quick start). But production requires:
- tiles/germany.mbtiles (not in repo; documented as user-generated)
- wireguard port, NET_ADMIN caps
- Caddy Let's Encrypt with localhost domains (would fail cert issuance but with DOMAIN_NAME=localhost as in docs example, Caddy uses internal? No — production Caddyfile uses automatic HTTPS; localhost would get internal cert automatically actually)

Hmm. Let me reconsider using the dev compose but fixing its bugs. Actually the task says "If the supplied guide provides multiple documented installation methods, do not declare the installation failed solely because one method fails." The dev method is documented. Its bugs: nginx mount path and qgis heredoc. But wait — are those really bugs, or is my compose version reading them differently? Let me double check the nginx mount: dev mounts `./nginx/nginx.conf` (which is the full nginx config with `worker_processes`) to `/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`. That IS wrong — the prod mounts nginx.conf to /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and default.conf to conf.d/default.conf. In dev, the dev file references `./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf` — clearly a bug since nginx.conf contains http{}. And it also doesn't mount default.conf. So dev nginx is broken as written.

And the qgis heredoc: `cat > ... <<EOF` with terminator on the same line as content, so the whole thing is one line and heredoc swallows the rest of the script (until EOF never appears as own line) — actually in the rendered command, the terminator `EOF` appears at end of line 4 ("...sslmode=disable EOF"), and there is no standalone EOF line, so the heredoc consumes everything after until... there's no EOF, so it consumes to end of input. That means the heredoc body becomes all subsequent commands, and the rest of the script (mkdir /var/www, nginx, spawn-fcgi, tail) never executes. The shell would then run cat, write the whole remaining script into pg_service.conf, and then... exit 0. Hence container exits 0 immediately and restarts. That's exactly the observed restarting (exit 0).

So the dev compose is definitively buggy. These are documentation/repo issues.

Given that, the documented production method is the better path. Let me try production compose. But it needs tiles/germany.mbtiles. The tileserver will fail without it. However, is tileserver essential to "installation success"? The app's core (frontend, API, admin, db, qgis) matters. But production compose won't fully start if tileserver keeps restarting (restart: always) — it won't block others though (no depends_on health for it except caddy depends_on tileserver service_started).

Also production backend build is same backend image (works). Production db uses our fixed Dockerfile. Nginx prod mounts correctly. QGIS prod uses printf (correct). Caddy prod uses Let's Encrypt; with DOMAIN_NAME=localhost etc, Caddy will attempt automatic HTTPS; localhost domains get internal CA automatically (Caddy treats localhost specially). Should work.

Wireguard requires NET_ADMIN/SYS_MODULE and /lib/modules — may fail, but it's optional-ish.

Given constraints, let me try production compose and see. But the db init.sh bug will bite on first run. Let me decide whether to fix init.sh. Since the bug prevents the first `up` from succeeding, and the guide's method is `docker-compose up -d`, a correct installation should not error. I think fixing init.sh is warranted as it's necessary to carry out the installation. But modifying repo source... The rules allow actions reasonably necessary. I already modified the postgres Dockerfile. Let me fix init.sh too to make the REVOKE tolerant.

Actually, let me reconsider: maybe I should stay with the dev stack and fix the two dev bugs, since the dev stack is simpler (no wireguard, no Let's Encrypt, no tileserver mbtiles requirement? Actually dev also uses tileserver with germany.mbtiles). Both need mbtiles.

The tiles issue is documented: mbtiles must be generated by the user. Without it the tileserver restarts. That's expected per docs ("user-generated, not included in repo"). So a fully working tileserver requires downloading ~germany OSM data (huge). Maybe generate a small region (berlin) to satisfy. But config.json references germany.mbtiles. We could generate berlin.mbtiles and update config.json. That's significant extra work but doable with Java + planetiler (needs java). Java may not be installed.

Let me step back and define "installation success" pragmatically: the application stack is deployed and core services run and are reachable. The tileserver is an optional basemap component requiring user-generated data not in the repo. I'll aim to get all services healthy where possible, and document tileserver as requiring user data.

Let me go with the production compose (primary documented method). First fix init.sh to not abort. Then bring up.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider whether fixing init.sh is "necessary". The first-run failure causes exit code 3, but then the second `up -d` succeeds because cluster exists. The installation still completes after retry. But is that acceptable? The guide expects a single command. To be robust, I'll fix init.sh.

Hmm, but is init.sh genuinely buggy for everyone, or only because tables don't exist yet? `REVOKE ALL ON model_permission` — table only exists after Django migrate. init.sh runs at DB init, before backend. So the REVOKE will ALWAYS fail on a fresh DB. That's a definite repo bug. It's surprising the project works at all... unless they expect ON_ERROR_STOP and... no, it's `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, so any error aborts. But the psql block containing REVOKE is the second heredoc; ON_ERROR_STOP causes psql to exit non-zero, and `set -e` aborts init.sh. So db init always fails on fresh install when QGIS creds set. Unless they don't set QGIS creds. Interesting. The .env.production.template sets QGIS_DB_USER. So production first-run fails too.

I'll make init.sh tolerate the missing relation. That is a reasonable fix to carry out the installation.

Let me now plan:
1. Fix init.sh (guard REVOKEs).
2. Reset postgres data dir.
3. Try production compose up -d --build.
4. Handle tileserver mbtiles.

Actually, maybe better to stick with dev compose since it's lighter (no wireguard, no Let's Encrypt, less memory). Production limits total ~14.9GB but host has 7.6GB RAM. Production db limit 6G, qgis 3G, backend 2G — sum exceeds RAM but Docker limits are caps, not reservations; actual usage may be lower. But 8 workers/6 workers etc. Risk of OOM. Dev compose is lighter. The guide lists dev method too.

Given host RAM 7.6GB, production compose is risky. Dev compose is the better fit and is documented. I'll fix the two dev bugs:
- nginx mount: change `./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro` to match prod style (mount nginx.conf -> /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and default.conf -> /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf).
- qgis heredoc: fix to printf form.

Wait, but is modifying the dev compose within scope? It's necessary to carry out installation via a documented method. Yes.

Hmm, but actually let me reconsider: maybe the intended "correct" method is production and the dev compose bugs are real repo bugs. But both stacks need fixes. Let me just pick dev (lighter) and fix it.

Actually, the guide's Quick Start at top says `docker-compose up -d --build` (production). The Installation.md guide is the primary source. Let me re-read the installation guide at top:

```
3. **Start services with Docker Compose**
   cd deployment
   docker-compose up -d --build
```

So the primary documented method is production compose. I should try that first. If it fails due to environment (RAM/caps/mbtiles), I fall back to dev.

Let me try production. But production db build uses same Dockerfile (fixed). Production also builds backend, frontend, caddy, pg-error-parser (already built). Pulls qgis, tileserver, nginx, wireguard.

Risk: wireguard needs /lib/modules and NET_ADMIN; in container likely fails to create WG interface → restart loop but won't block caddy (no depends_on).

Let me also consider Caddy prod: it needs ports 80/443 (free now). With APP_DOMAIN=app.localhost etc, Caddy auto-HTTPS uses internal CA for localhost domains. Good.

mbtiles: tileserver restart loop. Not blocking caddy.

Let me fix init.sh, reset data, and try production.

Wait, regarding host RAM: production qgis-server limits 3G, db 6G. Docker `deploy.resources.limits.memory` in compose v2 (non-swarm) is honored. With 7.6G total, if db actually uses ~2-3G and qgis ~1G, fine. Let's try.

Let me first fix init.sh.

Actually, do I even need to fix init.sh? Let me test: does the second `up` succeed? Yes it did in dev. So the "installation" completes on retry. But declaring success with a documented single-command failing on first run is questionable. I'll fix init.sh to be safe and make a clean single-command install work.

Let me look at the REVOKE lines and guard them.

The init.sh heredoc has `REVOKE ALL ON model_permission FROM "$QGIS_DB_USER";`. I'll replace with a DO block that checks to_regclass.

Let me edit.

Actually simpler: remove those two REVOKE lines? They're a security hardening for the QGIS user. But tables don't exist yet. Better: guard with a check. Use:
```
DO $$ BEGIN IF to_regclass('public.model_permission') IS NOT NULL THEN EXECUTE 'REVOKE ALL ON model_permission FROM "'||... 
```
Complicated with quoting. Simpler: use psql \gexec or just wrap:
```
SELECT 'REVOKE ALL ON model_permission FROM "' || '$QGIS_DB_USER' || '"' WHERE to_regclass('public.model_permission') IS NOT NULL \gexec
```
Hmm within heredoc. Alternatively, since the QGIS user is created before migrations, these permission tables don't exist. The intent is that QGIS user shouldn't read the permission tables. A cleaner approach: after Django migrations, run a management command. But minimal fix: make the REVOKEs conditional.

I'll use two separate psql invocations with `to_regclass` guard:

```
psql ... <<-EOSQL
DO $$
BEGIN
    IF to_regclass('public.model_permission') IS NOT NULL THEN
        EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON model_permission FROM %I', '$QGIS_DB_USER');
    END IF;
    IF to_regclass('public.route_permission') IS NOT NULL THEN
        EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON route_permission FROM %I', '$QGIS_DB_USER');
    END IF;
END
$$;
EOSQL
```

That's clean. Let me apply.

Hmm, but actually the REVOKE is inside the same big EOSQL block after ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES. I'll replace those two lines with the DO block.

Let me do it.

Let me proceed.
